q: Must a patient stop curative treatment to receive palliative care?
o: Yes - palliative care generally begins after disease-directed therapy has been abandoned
Yes - curative treatment usually needs to be stopped before palliative care begins
No - palliative care can accompany curative treatment
No - palliative care eligibility depends on enrollment in hospice
explanation: Palliative care is appropriate at any stage of serious illness and can accompany curative treatment (p1045). Abandonment or cessation of curative treatment is not a prerequisite, and hospice enrollment does not define eligibility. Only the unchanged key answers the question correctly.
chapterTitle: Palliative Care and Special Management Issues

q: What prognostic certification does the chapter describe for US Medicare hospice?
o: The hospice director alone certifies terminal illness and prognosis under 6 months if the disease runs its usual and expected course
An LCD automatically certifies terminal illness and prognosis under 6 months if the disease runs its usual and expected course
The attending physician and hospice director certify terminal illness and prognosis under 6 months if the disease runs its usual and expected course
The attending physician alone certifies terminal illness and prognosis under 6 months if the disease runs its usual and expected course
explanation:
Medicare hospice certification involves the attending physician and hospice medical director certifying terminal illness with prognosis under six months if the disease runs its usual and expected course (p1046).

D. The attending physician alone certifies terminal illness and prognosis under 6 months if the disease runs its usual and expected course: The described certification involves both physicians (p1046).
A. The hospice director alone certifies terminal illness and prognosis under 6 months if the disease runs its usual and expected course: The described certification involves both physicians (p1046).
B. An LCD automatically certifies terminal illness and prognosis under 6 months if the disease runs its usual and expected course: LCDs guide prognosis; they do not replace the described physician certification (p1046).

q: Are local coverage determinations strict hospice admission requirements?
o: Yes - meeting an LCD removes the need for terminal-illness certification
No - they guide prognosis and are not hospice admission requirements
No - they concern neither prognosis nor eligibility
Yes - they replace physician prognostic judgment
explanation:
Local coverage determinations guide prognosis but are not rules or requirements for hospice admission (p1046).

D. Yes - they replace physician prognostic judgment: They are guidelines to assist physicians in determining prognosis (p1046).
A. Yes - meeting an LCD removes the need for terminal-illness certification: The attending physician and hospice medical director must certify the terminal prognosis (p1046).
C. No - they concern neither prognosis nor eligibility: Their stated purpose is to help physicians determine prognosis (p1046).

q: What feeding approach is recommended in advanced dementia with dysphagia?
o: Routine percutaneous feeding tubes to prevent aspiration pneumonia
Oral assisted feeding
Routine percutaneous feeding tubes to improve pressure-ulcer healing
Routine percutaneous feeding tubes to improve survival
explanation:
Oral assisted feeding is recommended in advanced dementia; feeding tubes do not improve survival or prevent aspiration pneumonia (p1048).

D. Routine percutaneous feeding tubes to improve survival: Feeding tubes have not increased survival in advanced dementia (p1048).
A. Routine percutaneous feeding tubes to prevent aspiration pneumonia: Feeding tubes have not prevented aspiration pneumonia (p1048).
C. Routine percutaneous feeding tubes to improve pressure-ulcer healing: Feeding tubes have not improved healing and have been associated with pressure-ulcer development (p1048).

q: Does absence of a single terminal disease automatically exclude a frail patient from hospice?
o: No; prognosis can rest on the severity and irreversibility of frailty and multimorbidity
No; certification of a terminal prognosis is optional when frailty is present
Yes; the principal-diagnosis billing restriction generally makes frail patients ineligible
Yes; frailty with multimorbidity is insufficient grounds for a terminal prognosis
explanation: Frailty and multimorbidity may establish hospice eligibility without a single terminal illness if the attending physician and hospice medical director certify terminal illness with prognosis under six months. Severity and irreversibility inform that prognosis; the principal-diagnosis billing restriction does not bar the benefit (p1049). Thus optional certification, ineligibility from the billing restriction, and frailty being insufficient grounds are each wrong.

q: Why compare prognosis with time to benefit?
o: Short life expectancy tends to bring forward the benefit of preventive interventions
Preventive interventions generally spare frail patients immediate treatment harms
Life expectancy can be shorter than time to benefit, leaving only potential immediate harms
Prognosis is relevant to hospice selection but generally irrelevant to preventive treatment
explanation: Preventive benefit may take years; people whose life expectancy is shorter can incur immediate harms without receiving that benefit (p1050). Short prognosis does not accelerate benefit, immediate harms are possible, and prognosis is relevant to preventive treatment as well as hospice. Only the unchanged key states this time-to-benefit problem.

q: In which direction is clinicians' survival estimate commonly biased?
o: Toward overestimation by a factor of 3 to 5
Clinical estimates are entirely uncorrelated with actual survival
Toward underestimation by a factor of 3 to 5
No systematic bias is described
explanation:
Clinicians tend to overestimate survival by a factor of 3 to 5 (p1051).

C. Toward underestimation by a factor of 3 to 5: The stated direction is overestimation (p1051).
D. No systematic bias is described: The book describes numerous biases, particularly overestimation (p1051).
B. Clinical estimates are entirely uncorrelated with actual survival: The book says judgment-based estimates are correlated with survival despite bias (p1051).
